### Question 1

Everyone carries a private sense of what is fair — that private sense is your morals. Ethics is what happens when people stop simply feeling and start arguing: Is this fair? Why? Would it still be fair if the roles were reversed? Ethics is the reasoning and the justification, not the gut reaction. Law is what a government will actually enforce against you, and etiquette is polished behavior like introducing yourself before you touch someone. Four related ideas, four different jobs.

### Question 2

Picture a four-legged stool you sit on whenever a health care decision gets hard. One leg is letting the person decide for themselves. One is actively doing good for them. One is avoiding harm. One is treating everybody fairly. Honesty, promise-keeping, and confidentiality are real obligations too, but they rest on top of those legs rather than replacing them. Naming all four legs is how you check which one your decision is wobbling on.

### Question 3

A code of ethics is like the commitments a team writes and signs before the season: how we treat each other, what we will never do, who we intend to be. That is not the league rulebook that gets you ejected — the rulebook is the law, with referees and penalties. And the commitments do not tell you which play to call in the fourth quarter; they tell you what kind of team you promised to be while you figure the play out yourself.

### Question 4

Two teachers grade the same science project. The first only checks whether you followed the required procedure — correct method, full credit, no matter how the experiment turned out. That teacher is deontology, grading the duty. The second ignores your method and grades only the results and how useful they were. That is utilitarianism, grading the consequences. One project, two defensible grades — which is exactly why two people who both want to do right can reach opposite conclusions.

### Question 5

Most ethics questions sound like "What should I do right now?" Virtue ethics asks a harder one: "Who am I turning into?" Compare memorizing a card of plays for tonight's game with practicing daily until skill is simply part of you. Virtue ethics treats every choice as a repetition — each honest or courageous act builds a habit, and the habit is what shows up at 3 a.m. when no one hands you a card and there is no time to deliberate.

### Question 6

Think of a room. The law is the floor: you may not go below it, and if you do, someone with real authority stops you. Ethics is the ceiling, and it sits much higher. No statute requires you to explain a frightening test to a frightened patient gently rather than quickly, so you could do the legal minimum forever and never be sanctioned. But "I broke no rule" is a floor-level defense, and ethics asks you to stand up in the room, not merely stay off the ground.

### Question 7

Two nurses hear the same anxious question from a patient. A rule-driven approach asks first, "What is the standard answer every patient should get?" — valuable, because it treats people equally and resists favoritism. Care ethics asks a different question first: who is this particular person, what does this moment mean to them, and what does the relationship between us require right now? It is not rule-breaking. It is the claim that the specifics of the person in front of you are moral information, not noise to filter out.

### Question 8

Suppose a health department can fund exactly one of two campaigns and asks only one question: which one keeps more people out of the hospital? That is utilitarian reasoning — add up the expected good and take the bigger total. It is genuinely useful when you must decide for a whole population and cannot ask each person individually. It also carries a known catch: a bigger total can quietly conceal a group that received almost nothing, so naming the math is how you notice who was left out of the sum.

### Question 9

An ethics committee is a group you bring a genuinely tangled situation to when you want more minds on it. They surface angles you missed, they teach, and they help rewrite institutional policies that keep generating the same conflict. What they are not is a principal handing out punishment or a judge issuing a verdict you must obey. You go for better thinking and a clearer set of options; the decision still belongs to the patient, the surrogate, and the team.

### Question 10

Some safety rules only get written after something has already gone badly wrong. After decades in which researchers deceived Black men in Alabama and withheld treatment in order to study untreated syphilis, the country wrote down three ground rules for studying human beings: treat people as people who get to decide, weigh risks against benefits honestly, and choose participants fairly instead of choosing whoever is easiest to enroll. That is the Belmont Report — a lesson recorded so it would not have to be learned again.

### Question 11

A weather report tells you it is raining. It does not tell you to carry an umbrella — that is a separate step where someone gives advice and can be asked to justify it. Descriptive ethics is the weather report: here is what people in this group actually believe and actually do, measured. Normative ethics is the advice plus the argument behind it. Collapsing the two produces the classic mistake of thinking "everybody does it around here" settles whether it is right.

### Question 12

Suppose you promised a friend you would attend their game Saturday and also promised your grandmother you would help her move that same Saturday. Both promises are real; neither became fake just because they collided. You have to weigh them, choose, and be able to explain the choice — and the promise you set aside still leaves a residue, such as an apology or a make-up date you now owe. That is what prima facie means: binding on its face, overridable only for a genuinely stronger reason, never by a shrug.
